- **Time:** 80 minutes.
- **Slides:** [Documentation](../lectures/11-documentation/11-documentation.qmd)
- **You need:** the `ltee-project` after [lesson 10](10-nextflow.qmd).
- **You will have:** a README a stranger can follow, a license for each kind of material, a valid `CITATION.cff`, and `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`.
:::

## Overview

Git, Pixi, containers and workflows make an analysis *rerunnable*. Whether
anyone *does* rerun it, cite it or build on it depends on the documentation:
what the project is, where the data is, how to run it, what to expect, how to
cite it, and what others may do with it. Documentation is the fifth of the
five pillars of computational reproducibility (Ziemann et al. 2023), and like
the others it is written during the project, not at the end.

Our worked example is the LTEE project you have built since lesson 02 from the
course template: every file in it has a reason, and this lesson fills in the
parts a reader sees first.

### Learning outcomes

After this lesson you can:

1. **Write** a README that answers the seven questions a reader has (what, publication, contents, hardware, how to reproduce, outputs, contact).
2. **Choose and apply** licenses for code, text and data, and **explain** what each allows.
3. **Write** a valid `CITATION.cff` and **produce** a citation from it.
4. **Add** contributing and code-of-conduct files, and **record** software versions from the lock file.

Checks: `cffconvert --validate` passes (outcome 3); a classmate reproduces
your project from the README alone in [lesson 12](12-putting-it-together.qmd)
(outcome 1).

## 1. What a reader needs to know

The NBIS course lists seven questions a README must answer:

1. What is this project about?
2. Is there a publication related to it?
3. What is in this repository?
4. What hardware does it need?
5. How do I reproduce the analyses?
6. What outputs should I expect?
7. How can I contact the authors or discuss the project?

Look at your current README:

```{.bash .run}
cd ~/cbio7501/ltee-project
cat README.md
```

The template answered 3 (the folder table) and part of 5. Answer the rest
with what you now know about the project.

```{.bash .run-ci}
git switch -c lesson-11-documentation
```

## 2. Measure before you write

"Runs on a laptop" is not a hardware requirement. Measure: disk space of the
environments, the data and the results.

```{.bash .run}
du -sh .pixi/envs/* data/raw results
```

On our test laptop (Apple M4 Max, 2026-10-24) the environments took 3.6 GB,
the raw data 332 MB and the results 199 MB; the whole Snakemake workflow took
31 seconds on 4 cores, with at most 440 MB of memory (measured with
`/usr/bin/time -l` on macOS, `/usr/bin/time -v` on Linux).

## 3. The README

Replace `README.md` with this version and adapt the names, the numbers you
measured and the contact line. Keep it short: link to details instead of
repeating them.

````{.markdown filename="README.md" .write}
# LTEE variant calling

Variant calling on three *E. coli* clones from population Ara-3 of Richard
Lenski's Long-Term Evolution Experiment (LTEE), frozen at 5,000, 15,000 and
50,000 generations. Question: how many mutations accumulated, and is the
answer robust to the minimum read depth used to filter variant calls?

Built as the example project of the CBIO7501 Reproducible and Open Science
workshop. The analysis steps follow the Data Carpentry lesson *Wrangling
Genomics* (CC BY 4.0).

Author: Ada Lovelace (ORCID [0000-0002-1825-0097](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-1825-0097))

## Publication

None yet. The data and biology are from Tenaillon et al. (2016), *Nature*
536:165–170, <https://doi.org/10.1038/nature18959>.

## Reproduce the results

Requirements: [Pixi](https://pixi.prefix.dev/latest/) and an internet
connection. Linux or macOS (on Windows use WSL2: `bwa`, `samtools` and
`bcftools` have no Windows builds). No other installation is needed.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/ada-lovelace/ltee-project.git
cd ltee-project
pixi run reproduce
```

`pixi run reproduce` installs the exact software versions in `pixi.lock`,
downloads the raw data and checks its checksums, runs the Snakemake workflow
and renders the report. A GitHub Action runs the same command on every push.

Other entry points: `pixi run run-nextflow` (the same pipeline in Nextflow),
`pixi run compare-workflows` (checks that both give identical variant calls),
`pixi task list` (all tasks).

A container image of the pipeline environment can be built from
`containers/Dockerfile` (see the comments in that file).

## Hardware

Any laptop from the last few years. Measured on 2026-10-24 (Apple M4 Max,
4 cores): about 4 GB of disk for the software environments, 330 MB for the
raw data and 200 MB for the results; the workflow takes under a minute and
less than 1 GB of memory.

## Outputs

| Path | Content |
|------|---------|
| `reports/ltee-report.html` | The report: data, read quality, variants, the depth sensitivity analysis, software versions |
| `results/qc/multiqc/multiqc_report.html` | Read quality summary |
| `results/vcf/` | Filtered variant calls per sample (minimum depth from `config/config.yaml`) |
| `results/sensitivity/` | Variant calls at each depth in `sensitivity_depths` |
| `results/stats/` | Alignment (`flagstat`) and variant (`bcftools stats`) statistics |

Expected filtered variants at minimum depth 2: SRR2589044 10, SRR2584863 25,
SRR2584866 775.

## Data

Raw reads: a subset of three runs prepared by Data Carpentry, figshare,
<https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.7726454> (file `sub.tar.gz`, CC0).
Original runs in NCBI BioProject PRJNA295606. Reference: *E. coli* B str.
REL606, GenBank CP000819.1. Sources, provider checksums and our checksums are
in `metadata/`; the data is not stored in this repository.

## Repository contents

See the table in `docs/structure.md` (each folder also has its own README).

## Cite

See `CITATION.cff` (GitHub: "Cite this repository").

## License

Code: MIT (`LICENSE`). Report text and figures: CC BY 4.0. The raw data is
CC0 (see Data).

## Contact

Questions and problems: open an issue on GitHub. Contributions: see
`CONTRIBUTING.md`. Everyone taking part follows `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`.
````

The folder table from the template moves to `docs/structure.md`, so the README
stays short. Save it there:

````{.markdown filename="docs/structure.md" .write}
# Project structure

| Folder | What goes in it | Rule |
|--------|-----------------|------|
| `data/raw/` | Raw data, downloaded by `scripts/download_data.py` | Read-only, not committed |
| `data/processed/` | Data derived from raw data (decompressed, indexed reference) | Rebuilt by the workflow |
| `metadata/` | Sample sheet, data sources, checksums, data dictionary | Committed |
| `scripts/` | Download, comparison and helper code | Committed |
| `config/` | Workflow settings (`config.yaml`), shared by Snakemake and Nextflow | Committed |
| `workflow/` | `Snakefile` and `nextflow/` | Committed |
| `notebooks/` | Exploration (`explore-reads.ipynb`), outputs cleared | Committed |
| `reports/` | Quarto report source and bibliography | Source committed, HTML not |
| `results/` | Everything the workflow produces | Rebuilt, not committed |
| `docs/` | This file, the decision log | Committed |
| `envs/` | Conda exports of the Pixi environments | Generated |
| `containers/` | `Dockerfile` and `apptainer.def`, built from `pixi.lock` | Committed |
| `.github/workflows/` | The reproduce-from-a-clean-clone check | Committed |
````

## 4. Licenses: what others may do

Without a license, others may read your public code but not legally reuse it.
Pick licenses deliberately, one per kind of material:

| Material | Common choice | What it allows |
|----------|---------------|----------------|
| Code | MIT, BSD-3-Clause, Apache-2.0 (permissive); GPL-3.0 (copyleft: derived code must stay open under the GPL) | Permissive: reuse anywhere, keep the notice |
| Text, figures, slides | CC BY 4.0 | Reuse and adapt with credit |
| Data | CC0 (no conditions) or CC BY 4.0 | CC0 is easiest to combine with other data |
| Things to avoid for open research | "NC" (non-commercial) and "ND" (no derivatives) Creative Commons licenses | They block much reuse, including some teaching and journals |

The template put the license you chose in `LICENSE` (MIT by default):

```{.bash .run}
head -3 LICENSE
```

The README says which license covers what (code MIT, report text CC BY 4.0,
data CC0 from its provider). You may only license what you own: the LTEE data
keeps the license figshare gives it, and the Data Carpentry steps keep their
credit. [choosealicense.com](https://choosealicense.com/) explains the
software licenses in plain language.

## 5. A citation file

`CITATION.cff` tells people and machines how to cite the project; GitHub turns
it into a "Cite this repository" button and Zenodo reads it for its record
(lesson 12). Replace the template's version with a complete one (use your own
name and ORCID iD; this example uses ORCID's documentation test ID):

```{.yaml filename="CITATION.cff" .write}
cff-version: 1.2.0
message: "If you use this work, please cite it as below."
title: "LTEE variant calling"
abstract: "Variant calling on three E. coli clones from the Long-Term Evolution Experiment, with a sensitivity analysis of the variant filter."
type: software
authors:
  - given-names: "Ada"
    family-names: "Lovelace"
    email: "ada@example.org"
    orcid: "https://orcid.org/0000-0002-1825-0097"
repository-code: "https://github.com/ada-lovelace/ltee-project"
license: MIT
version: 0.1.0
date-released: "2026-12-01"
keywords:
  - reproducibility
  - variant calling
  - Long-Term Evolution Experiment
references:
  - type: article
    title: "Tempo and mode of genome evolution in a 50,000-generation experiment"
    authors:
      - family-names: "Tenaillon"
        given-names: "Olivier"
      - name: "et al."
    journal: "Nature"
    volume: 536
    start: 165
    end: 170
    year: 2016
    doi: "10.1038/nature18959"
```

Check it, and see what a citation made from it looks like:

```{.bash .run}
pixi exec cffconvert --validate -i CITATION.cff
pixi exec cffconvert -i CITATION.cff -f apalike
pixi exec cffconvert -i CITATION.cff -f bibtex
```

## 6. Contributing and conduct

Two short files tell others how to take part. `CONTRIBUTING.md`:

```{.markdown filename="CONTRIBUTING.md" .write}
# Contributing

Thank you for helping. This is a small research project, so the process is simple:

1. Open an issue describing the problem or idea before larger changes.
2. Fork the repository, make a branch, and check that `pixi run reproduce`
   still works on your computer.
3. Open a pull request. The *Reproduce* check must pass before merging.

Please keep raw data out of Git (`data/raw/` is downloaded by
`scripts/download_data.py`), commit `pixi.toml` and `pixi.lock` together, and
record analysis decisions in `docs/decisions.md`.
```

`CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`: most projects adopt an existing code rather than write
their own. Point to the Contributor Covenant and say who to contact:

```{.markdown filename="CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md" .write}
# Code of conduct

Everyone taking part in this project (issues, pull requests, discussions)
follows the Contributor Covenant, version 3.0:
<https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/3/0/code_of_conduct/>.

Report unacceptable behaviour to ada@example.org. Reports are handled
confidentially.
```

## 7. Software versions, for humans

`pixi.lock` records every package for machines. For a methods section or a
reviewer, list the versions you actually used. Pixi prints them; keep the list
with the documentation:

```{.bash .run}
pixi list -e pipeline --explicit > docs/software-versions.txt
grep -E "^(bwa|samtools|bcftools|fastqc|multiqc|snakemake|nextflow|python|quarto) " docs/software-versions.txt
```

```text
bcftools    1.24     ...
bwa         0.7.19   ...
...
```

The report prints its own key versions (lesson 07), so the methods and the
results can never disagree.

## 8. Comments and the workflow picture

Documentation also lives in the code: the header comments of the Snakefile and
`main.nf` say where the steps come from, `config/config.yaml` explains every
setting, and `docs/decisions.md` records why. Add the rule graph to the docs:

```{.bash .run}
pixi run -e pipeline snakemake --rulegraph > docs/rulegraph.dot
pixi run -e pipeline dot -Tsvg docs/rulegraph.dot -o docs/rulegraph.svg
```

(If Graphviz says `Format: "svg" not recognized`, run `pixi run -e pipeline dot -c`
once, as in lesson 09.)

## Break it: a citation file GitHub cannot read

A typo in `CITATION.cff` silently removes the "Cite this repository" button.
Introduce one (an ORCID iD without the `https://orcid.org/` part):

```{.bash .run}
cp CITATION.cff CITATION.cff.bak
sed 's|orcid: "https://orcid.org/0000-0002-1825-0097"|orcid: "0000-0002-1825-0097"|' CITATION.cff.bak > CITATION.cff
grep orcid CITATION.cff
```

```{.bash .expect-fail}
pixi exec cffconvert --validate -i CITATION.cff
```

```text
jsonschema.exceptions.ValidationError: '0000-0002-1825-0097' does not match 'https://orcid\\.org/[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{3}[0-9X]{1}'
On instance['orcid']:
```

Restore it, and validate again:

```{.bash .run}
mv CITATION.cff.bak CITATION.cff
pixi exec cffconvert --validate -i CITATION.cff
```

Validate the citation file in CI too, so a typo cannot slip in unnoticed (one
more step in `.github/workflows/reproduce.yml`, see Try it yourself).

## Try it yourself

1. Add a step to `.github/workflows/reproduce.yml` that validates `CITATION.cff`.

   ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
   After the "Install Pixi" step:
   ```yaml
         - name: Citation file is valid
           run: pixi exec cffconvert --validate -i CITATION.cff
   ```
   :::

2. A reader asks: "Which version of samtools made Figure 2?" Where in your
   project is the answer? Give two places.

   ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
   `pixi.lock` (exact package and checksum, per platform) and
   `docs/software-versions.txt` (human-readable); the report also prints key
   versions. With the Git commit of the report, the answer is exact.
   :::

## Save your work

```{.bash .run-ci}
git add README.md docs/structure.md docs/software-versions.txt docs/rulegraph.svg CITATION.cff CONTRIBUTING.md CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md
git commit -m "Document the project: README, citation, contributing and conduct"
git push -u origin lesson-11-documentation
```

Open the pull request, check the "Cite this repository" button on the branch
page, and merge.

## Troubleshooting

| Problem | What to do |
|---------|------------|
| No "Cite this repository" button on GitHub | `CITATION.cff` must be in the repository root, on the default branch, and valid: run `cffconvert --validate`. |
| `cffconvert: command not found` | Run it through Pixi: `pixi exec cffconvert ...`. |
| Unsure which license to pick | Code: MIT unless your institution or funder says otherwise. Text: CC BY 4.0. Ask your library or tech-transfer office for anything with patents or personal data. |
| The README commands no longer work | Documentation must be tested like code: rerun the README's commands in a fresh clone (lesson 12 does this with a classmate). |

## Apply it to your own project

Write your capstone README with the seven sections, add `CITATION.cff` and
validate it, choose licenses for code, text and data (and check you may share
your data at all), and add `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`.

## Key points

- A README answers seven questions: what, publication, contents, hardware, how to reproduce, outputs, contact.
- Measure hardware needs; state the one command that reproduces everything.
- License code, text and data separately; you can only license what you own.
- `CITATION.cff` makes the project citable on GitHub and Zenodo; validate it.
- Software versions come from the lock file, not from memory.
